uprising

/UP-rye-zing/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Uprising means an act of rebellion in which a group of people rises up, often suddenly, against the authority that rules them.

When the royal tax collectors doubled their demands for the third year in a row, the colonial farmers answered with an uprising that drove them from the county.

Example

The uprising at the overcrowded prison ended only after the warden agreed to restore visiting hours and improve the food.

The prisoners rose up together against the authority controlling them — the warden — to force a change. A group challenging the power that rules them is exactly what an uprising is.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

revolt: A revolt is an organized refusal to keep obeying an authority, and it can stay bloodless or even figurative — shareholders revolt, taxpayers revolt. An uprising is more physical and more sudden: people rising in a body against the power over them, usually in the streets rather than on paper.

rebellion: Rebellion is open resistance to a government or ruler, and it can name a long condition — a countryside in rebellion for years. An uprising is an event: sudden, datable, something that breaks out on a particular night. Rebellion is the state of resisting; an uprising is the eruption itself.

insurrection: An insurrection is a violent attempt to overthrow those in power and take control — the word aims at toppling and seizing. An uprising rises against an authority but may want change rather than the throne: prisoners staging an uprising want better food, not the warden's office.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

submission: yielding to the will of an authority

obedience: doing what those in power command

Where it sits · how far the challenge to power goes

protest → uprising → revolution

protest vs. uprising: A protest voices anger at those in power; an uprising takes direct action against them.

revolution vs. uprising: An uprising challenges the people in charge; a revolution goes further and overthrows the entire system.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — up-: upward, into action (Old English)

Root — rise: to get up, to ascend (Old English risan)

Suffix — -ing: forms a noun naming an act or event

Put it together: Up + rise + -ing literally names the act of rising up — a group of people getting up off their knees to stand against the power that rules them.

Use the root in a new word: arise: Problems can arise quickly when no one checks the plan twice.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral - news & history

An uprising is usually local and aimed at a specific authority (a governor, an occupying army, a prison warden); a revolution is larger and replaces the whole system. You will often see the matching verb phrase "rise up": the people rose up, and the uprising spread.
